title: The three lines: right, left, and the middle line that reaches the inner Keser
overview:
In *Tikun* the *sefiros* stand as a *partzuf* in three lines. On the right, *chachma*, *chesed* and *netzach*: *chachma* looks past the outside to what it stands for, "it's the thought that counts", and so leans to kindness. On the left, *bina*, *gevura* and *hod*: *bina* looks at the outside, draws distinctions, and is nitpicky. Each branch is separate from its source, which is why a high-minded idea loses force by the time it has to go out knocking on doors in the cold.

The two sides come together only through the middle line. *Daas* sees both as tools and makes a judgment call for this person, a human thing no computer can do; *tiferes* is mercy after the verdict, Yaakov's way of giving a ladder out of the mud; *yesod* decides between *netzach* and *hod*, the kidneys that say yes and no. The middle line can join them because it reaches the inner *Keser*, the will with no reason, all or nothing. The *paroches* is where that will takes a form, so prayer goes before it to change judgement to kindness.

terms.gloss: lines: the three lines of a partzuf, chachma, chesed and netzach on the right, bina, gevura and hod on the left, daas, tiferes and yesod in the middle
the Keser within the Keser: the inner, essential will, which does not split into lines
acknowledgement: holding back, caution, giving up one's strength before what is bigger
the daas that tilts: it sees both sides and decides how much of each, for this person and this situation
mercy: it comes after the verdict, and lets the person off because the goal is that he improve
the kidneys that advise: netzach and hod, which say yes and no on how to carry out a decision
the weighing of the mind: the whole middle line, which makes a judgment call
the middle bar: the pole through all the boards of the Mishkan; the middle line, one through every level
the hidden reason for the will: chachma of Keser, hidden because the will covers it, and really a taste of delight
the days of old: the middos of the will and delight, the original dream before it is brought down to what is possible
the curtain between the Holy and the Holy of Holies: the screen between the essential will and the will that has a form
the membrane of air, which he calls the arachnoid membrane: the screen through which the essential delight reaches the faculties

sections.title: Three lines: the inner Keser does not divide, its outer side does
sections.summary: In *Tikun* the *sefiros* stand as a *partzuf* (a stature) in three lines, right, left and middle. The inner *Keser*, the essential will, does not split into lines; from its outer side, already *chachma* of *Keser*, they divide.

phrases.he: (כא) ובזה יובן כללות ענין ההתכללות דג' קוין דנאצלים,
חח''ן מימין ובג''ה משמאל ודת''י באמצע כו'
phrases.en: that when the *sefiros* go out, *chachma*, *chesed*, *netzach* is on the right, *bina*, *gevura*, *hod* is on the left, and then *daas*, *tiferes*, *yesod* stays in the middle.

blocks.text: He now explains the three *kavin* (lines): how the *sefiros* (the Divine attributes) split into three lines. In *Tohu* (the world of Chaos) they are separate *nekudos* (points); in *Tikun* (the world of repair) they become a *partzuf* (lit. face; a stature of the *sefiros*), and a *partzuf* means three lines: *chachma* (wisdom), *chesed* (kindness) and *netzach* (victory) on the right; *bina* (understanding), *gevura* (might, restraint) and *hod* (acknowledgement) on the left; *daas* (knowledge), *tiferes* (beauty) and *yesod* (foundation) in the middle.

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב בפרדס דפנימית הכתר הנקרא כתר שבכתר,
לא נחלק לג' קוין
phrases.en: That doesn't split up into three *kavin*.

phrases.he: בחינת חיצוניות שבו,
phrases.en: but from the *chitzoniyus* of the *ratzon* already,

phrases.he: ממנו מתחלק לג' קוין
והוא מבחינת חכמה שבכתר כו', וכידוע בכונות דהגדול הגבור והנורא כו'.

blocks.text: As the *Pardes* says, the *pnimiyus* (the inner side) of *Keser*, called *Keser sheb'Keser*, is the inner *ratzon* (will) itself, like the *nekuda* (the point): the *etzem* (essence) of what you want. It does not split into three lines. From the *chitzoniyus* (the outer side) of the will it already divides, becoming like a *partzuf* in *yosher* (the straight line); as we said of *Arich Anpin*, it becomes *yosher* *davka* (specifically) in the form of *Chabad* and the six *middos* (emotional attributes).

This is from *chachma* of *Keser*, as is known from the *kavanos* (intentions) of "the great, the mighty and the awesome", the three lines in *Keser*: "the great" is *chesed*, "the mighty" is *gevura*, and the *heh* ("the") is in a way a *hispashtus* (spreading forth).

sections.title: The right line and the left: chachma looks past the form, bina at it
sections.summary: On the right, *chesed* is a branch of *chachma* and *netzach* a branch of *chesed*, each separate from its source; on the left, *bina*, *gevura* and *hod* are the opposite. *Chachma* looks past the outside to what it stands for and so leans to kindness; *bina* looks at the outside, makes distinctions and leans to judgement.

phrases.he: וביאור הדברים, הנה בחינת התכללות הקוין ימין ושמאל הוא על ידי קו האמצעי דוקא
phrases.en: The right and the left lines are connected through the middle line.

blocks.text: The explanation of the matter: the inclusion of the lines, right and left, is *davka* through the middle line. The right and the left lines are connected only through the middle line.

phrases.he: והענין הוא דקו הימין חח''ן, הרי החסד ענף החכמה ומובדל הימנה
phrases.en: On the right line, *chesed* is a branch of *chachma*, but it's separate from it.

phrases.he: והוא מה שנסתעף החסד מצד השכל והטעם, שמטה כלפי חסד
phrases.en: This is when, because of a reason, you lean towards *chesed*.

phrases.he: בדבר מורכב כנזכר לעיל

blocks.text: On the right line, **chesed is a branch of chachma, but it's separate from it**. It branches out from the intellect and the reason: **because of a reason, you lean towards chesed**. It is not an *etzem chesed* (essential kindness); your *sechel* (intellect) causes the *chesed*.

blocks.title: The right hand gives
blocks.text: The right arm is on the same side as the right side of the brain. You usually hold things with your left hand, and take and give with your right. That is one reason the right hand is a *mashal* (analogy) for *chesed*, on the same side as *chachma*.

In general *chachma* leans towards *chesed*. The *inyan* (concept) of *chachma* is to look behind the *chitzoniyus*, past the form, at the abstract thing it represents; *bina* looks at the external form. So *chachma* leans towards *chesed*, and *bina* towards *gevura*.

blocks.title: It's the thought that counts
blocks.text: As we said before: someone gives a gift, and you look into it and say, "It's the thought that counts." That is *chachma*: you look deeper, at what it represents, and you appreciate it very much.

blocks.title: Looking past a person's deeds
blocks.text: So with a person. Even if outwardly he is not so good, and what he is doing isn't good, you look past it, at his inner motivation, at how inside he is a person like you. You can relate to him: really he is just misguided. That is *chachma*.

*Bina* focuses on the external. Focus there and you will never find a gift that properly represents the love you want to express. Be *medakdek* (exacting) about the outside and "it's never going to be perfect. You're always going to find the flaw."

So with a person: "there is no righteous man on earth". Be exacting about his actions, especially about how he lives up to what you could expect of him, and you will always find something wrong. "That's true."

You can look at it either way. *Chachma* says: since the feeling can never be properly represented in the outside thing, look past it. It's the thought that counts; the *etzem* connection is there, and how we express it doesn't really matter.

*Bina* looks at the outside and says, "But I want it to come out": make the effort to make a meaningful expression of what you want to convey; act in a way befitting who you really are, that expresses our relationship. "It's very nitpicky." So *chachma* leans towards *chesed*.

blocks.title: The poor person
blocks.text: Say a person looks at a poor man. From the side of *chachma* he feels he should be nice to him: he finds common ground, relates to him and sympathizes, and so he wants to give him *tzedaka* (charity); or he understands intellectually that it is good to be nice to him.

phrases.he: וכן הנצח ענף החסד,
phrases.en: and likewise, *netzach* is an *anaf* of *chesed*,

phrases.he: מובדל הימנו.
phrases.en: but it's also separate from the *chesed*.

phrases.he: דהיינו מצד החסד יחויב בחינת הניצוח להביא החסד למעשה בפועל ממש כו'

blocks.text: Likewise *netzach* is an *anaf* (a branch) of *chesed*, and also separate from it. *Chesed* requires *netzach* to bring it to actual deed. *Chesed* is *hispashtus*, wanting to get something out; but when you want to express or give something to someone in deed, there is definitely going to be opposition, and you have to figure out how to do it. That is *netzach*.

blocks.title: The father teaching his son
blocks.text: You always have to fight the *kli* (vessel), like the *mashal* in *Tanya* of a father teaching his son. From *chesed* he wants to give his son what he knows, his *chachma*, but it is hard: he has to bring it down to the son's level. *Netzach* is the work of overcoming the language barrier and the different backgrounds, to bring it across in a way the other will appreciate.

blocks.title: Running after him to help
blocks.text: The simple case is the right leg. If a person wants to do *chesed* for a guy, the *chesed* obligates him even to run after the guy to help him: that is really a *netzach* thing. If there is an obstacle, the *chesed* says, "Really you should even have *netzach*; you should even be willing to fight for what's right."

But, as he is going to say, the right and left lines are detached. So in theory a person can be very high-minded from the side of his *chachma*; in the emotion he is less enthusiastic, and by *netzach*, actually running after somebody, a lot less. Still it obligates him: a person should do these things.

blocks.title: Mivtzaim in the cold
blocks.text:
Like *mivtzaim* (outreach campaigns). From *chachma* a person sees that it is right to help other Jews, and he feels a *chesed*, that they should be helped. Actually going and doing it, when it is difficult, is *netzach*: overcoming obstacles to raise money and get the things, the time, the cold, finding the people. For a lot of people it is uncomfortable to go around knocking on doors giving out menorahs.

The *chesed* obligates it, but it is detached, so it loses some of its *koach* (power), as he is going to say.

phrases.he: וקו השמאל היפוכו,
phrases.en: the left line is the opposite of everything in the right line,

phrases.he: כמו שכל המטה כלפי דין שנסתעף הימנו מידת הדין כו'
כך בינה גבורה כו'
phrases.en: So too is *bina gevura*, that *bina* leans towards *gevura*,

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב אני בינה, לי גבורה כו'
phrases.en: I am *bina* and *gevura* is mine,

phrases.he: דהחכמה נוטה לחסדים
ובינה מינה דינין כו'
phrases.en: that from *bina* comes out *dinin*.

phrases.he: (וכמו שכתוב בעץ חיים דאבא מקור החסדים
phrases.en: that *Abba*'s the source of the *chassadim*.

phrases.he: ואימא מקור כל הגבורות כו' וכידוע)
phrases.en: and *Ima* is the *makor* of all the *gevuros*

blocks.text: The left line is the opposite of the right: an intellect that leans towards *din* (judgement), from which the attribute of judgement branches out. So too *bina* leans towards *gevura*, as it says, "I am *bina*, *gevura* is mine." For *chachma* leans to the *chassadim* (kindnesses), and from *bina* the *dinin* (judgements) come out.

As it says in *Etz Chaim*, *Abba* is the source of the *chassadim*. *Chachma* grasps the *mahus* (the what-it-is), the abstract, and that always causes *chassadim*: understanding something with *chachma*, you see how it applies to everything and how things connect. Its nature is always to break barriers and go deeper and deeper, to the essence, which transcends boundaries and limitations.

*Bina* is the opposite: to define, compartmentalize and draw sharp distinctions. To talk, you need *bina* to find words that name exactly what you want to say, so people get it. But to really understand what a person is saying you also need *chachma*, to read between the lines and pull out what he really means. You need both.

blocks.title: Living the story
blocks.text: Take a person reading. (Later we will talk about how *chachma* and *bina* deal with language, thought and speech.) Knowing the literal definition of the words is *bina*. When he doesn't even realize he is reading anymore, as if he is living the story, that is *chachma*: it becomes totally transparent. That is the *pnimiyus* of the *mochin* (the intellectual faculties), *mamash* (actually) one with its thing.

And *Ima* is the source of all the *gevuros*, because *bina* makes distinctions and breaks things up. It looks at the *chitzoniyus*, only the *gilui* (revelation) and not the *etzem*, and that itself is limited, the *inyan* of *gevuros*. And it cuts things up, using a part to represent the whole; later we will talk about the five *gevuros*, the final letters *mem*, *nun*, *tzadi*, *peh*, *chaf*.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 78 opens by finishing line 12, which class 77 ended in the middle of.

sections.title: The middle line: daas sees both sides and makes a judgment call
sections.summary: Two ways of looking at anything, past the outside or at it, come together only through *daas*. *Daas* holds both as tools and decides, for this person and this situation, how much of each: a human, subjective judgment no computer can make.

phrases.he: ובחינת ההתכללות דב' קוין הללו שיבואו להתחבר במקום א',
הוא על ידי קו האמצעי דת''י כו'
phrases.en: it's *davka* the middle thing, which is *daas*.

blocks.question: How can *chachma* and *bina*, or *chesed* and *gevura*, come together?
blocks.text: Whenever you approach any situation there are these two sides: you can look at it one way or the other. So which way do you look at it?

blocks.title: Avraham saw their inner good
blocks.text: You could look at a person as Avraham did. He saw their inner good: even when they were doing bad things, he realized they were moved by an inner good desire and just expressed it badly, and he appreciated their inner potential. You can overlook a person's shortcomings and always see the good, overlook that he isn't acting appropriately. Or you could look with *bina*, at the *chitzoniyus*. Neither really detracts from the other.
They are two totally different ways of looking at things. So to have them together, it is *davka* the middle thing, which is *daas*.

phrases.he: כמו הדעת שהוא בחינת ממוצע להטות משכל של חסד לשכל של דין, ונקרא דעת נוטה

blocks.text: Like *daas*, the intermediary that tilts from an intellect of *chesed* to an intellect of *din*, called *daas noteh* (the *daas* that tilts). *Daas* recognizes both. On one side the inner thing is good, the thought counts: say a parent with a child, an essential connection. On the other, "I don't like the way the person's acting; it makes me uncomfortable." *Daas* can understand both, be *sovel* (bear) both.

And it sees what is best for this person in this situation: how to get him to acknowledge his potential, that it is always there, and that he will never bring it out perfectly, "nobody's perfect. But I want you to work to bring this out and express it as best as you can." It tailors it: which side to focus on, in what proportion. "So it's a judgment call."

*Daas* is *davka* personal: an opinion, a human thing. "You couldn't have a computer make a decision on the level of *daas*." *Chachma* and *bina* are technical; *daas* asks what our real goal is. It sees both sides as tools to motivate and accomplish things, and takes whichever side, or combination, will be most effective. That is *daas noteh*.

phrases.he: (וכמו כי יצר לב כו'
phrases.en: like with the *Mabul*,

phrases.he: שנעשה שכל וטעם לזכות, אשר תחלה היה זה השכל עצמו נוטה כלפי חוב, כמו שכתוב וירא כי רבה רעת כו' וכהאי גוונא וכמו שכתוב במקום אחר)

blocks.text: Like "the inclination of the heart" at the *Mabul* (the Flood): the same fact, that man is born bad, served both *chesed* and *din*. The intellect of *chesed* says, so it is not their fault if they sin; the intellect of *gevura* says, but they are sinning, so that is bad. The same reason became a reason to acquit, where at first it leaned towards guilt, as it says, "And He saw that the evil of man was great."
Everything has two ways you can look at it, and you have to choose which way you are going to look at it. That is *daas*: an opinion, a subjective thing.

phrases.he: ונמצא בדעת יחובר ב' שכליים הפכיים דחסד וגבורה להיות נוטה לחסד באופן זה ולדין באופן זה וכהאי גוונא, גם במקום אחד

blocks.text: So in *daas* the two opposite intellects of *chesed* and *gevura* are joined, to lean to *chesed* in this way and to *din* in that way. *Daas* says both are true: up to a point we overlook it, and past it we don't. It is a judgment: a little thing, depending on the person and the situation, you overlook; but you expect a certain amount to come out, a certain effort.

This is what we said about the *Kav* (the line of light): the teacher has to measure how much effort he will put out and how much he wants from the student; how far you come down to the person, and how far he has to work to come to you. That decision is *davka* a thing of *daas*.

Even in one situation it is not all or nothing: you can help a little and at the same time make him work a little. It does not go 100% one way or 100% the other; it can make a compromise. The middle line is individualized, a human thing.

sections.title: Tiferes is mercy after the verdict: the attribute of Yaakov
sections.summary: *Tiferes* decides between *chesed* and *gevura* as mercy does: it comes only after judgement, when the person is guilty, and lets him off because the goal is that he improve. That is Yaakov's attribute: give as much help as is needed until he can stand on his own.

phrases.he: וכך מדת התפארת מכריע בין חסד וגבורה
phrases.en: the same way that *tiferes*, which is like a thing of mercy, is an intermediary between *chesed* and *gevura*.

phrases.he: שהוא כמו הרחמים,
phrases.en: which that's like mercy,

phrases.he: שאינו אלא אחר מידת הדין,
phrases.en: that after a person is guilty, and there's a problem,

phrases.he: שעם כל זה רחמנות פוטרו,
והיא מדת יעקב כידוע
phrases.en: it's the *midda* of Yaakov,

blocks.text: So too **tiferes, which is like a thing of mercy, is an intermediary between chesed and gevura**. Mercy comes only after judgement: **after a person is guilty, and there's a problem**, mercy still lets him off. "I beg the mercy of the court": you ask for mercy after he was found guilty.

*Rachmanus* (mercy) means you recognize a certain good in the person; if there were no hope, no good in him, you would feel only *gevura*. You see the good, and see it being messed up, and still say, "Sometimes I'm going to overlook it, because the person needs the help." Since my real goal is to help him, it is not about a judgment system: "it's not really about who's right. The point is to get the person to improve."

blocks.title: Tests, scores and three strikes
blocks.text: Say a teacher has tests with scores, or three strikes you're out. The system exists so that the student has to work and the responsibility is on him. Say he worked really hard and it didn't work out. From *din* you say, "It doesn't matter. These are the rules": if I let people off, they won't work and won't learn. So sometimes you have to say, "I don't care," and even be harsh *davka*, to make an example that inspires others to work.

blocks.title: The student below the level of the class
blocks.text: But if it is private and nobody will know, then especially you can let it go. Say someone is way below the level of the class. If he really wants to improve he won't care about his grade; even if he fails, as long as he is learning he will be happy. A teacher who appreciates that maybe shouldn't send him to the higher class, "but whatever", and definitely shouldn't punish him for not passing. That *rachmanus* is *davka* an intermediary between *chesed* and *gevura*, a human thing that comes from *daas*, subjective.

It is **the midda of Yaakov**. Yaakov says: I see that you have potential and good, and I see that you have problems. I will come down and give you as much help as you need, but the objective is that you be able to go on your own.

blocks.title: A ladder out of the mud
blocks.text: Like giving a person a ladder: you are not going to take him out of the mud and that's it; you help him pull himself out, with as much help as he needs to rehabilitate, until he can stand on his own. That is the way of Yaakov, as is known.

sections.title: Yesod between netzach and hod: the kidneys that advise yes and no
sections.summary: *Netzach* and *hod* are the counsel on how to carry a decision out: *netzach* says to give and be proactive, *hod* to hold back and be cautious, like the kidneys that advise yes and no. *Yesod* decides between them, after the first decision of *daas*.

phrases.he: וכן בחינת יסוד
phrases.en: also *yesod*,

phrases.he: ממוצע לכלול ב' הפכים דנצח והוד

blocks.title: Spoon-feeding the student, or holding back
blocks.text:
So too *yesod* includes the two opposites, *netzach* and *hod*. Say you are teaching. *Netzach*, wanting to bring the idea to the student, does all the work for him: explains everything simply, lays it all out, and he has nothing to do. The good: he will get it. The problem: he won't get to a higher level or learn to think on his own; he will "just become dependent on a good teacher."

*Hod* wants to inspire him to work harder: it asks hard questions, makes him think, and holds back some of the information, keeping it above him so that he wants to work to get it.

phrases.he: שהוא ענין כליות יועצות
phrases.en: *netzach* and *hod* is like the kidneys that give advice,

phrases.he: הן ולאו
phrases.en: that they say yes and no.

phrases.he: קודם השפעת המשפיע
כשצריך להשפיע עצם המדות חסד וגבורה
phrases.en: then when you want to bring across *chesed* and *gevura*,

blocks.title: The kidney and the glands on top of it
blocks.text: *Netzach* and *hod* are *kelayos yo'atzos*, the kidneys that give advice, that say yes and no. The kidney, from what Rabbi Walters researched, has three parts, as every organ the Torah talks about does, for *Chabad*, *chagas* and *nehi* (the three triads of *sefiros*). What English calls the kidney is only the bottom third; on top are two stacked adrenal glands, the top one tied to the pituitary gland, working with the brain to regulate the body.

sensitivity.reason: Describes the adrenal glands as two glands stacked on the kidney, the top one tied to the pituitary, as anatomy from his own research; loose as medicine, and a reader may take it as fact.
sensitivity.publishable: *Netzach* and *hod* are *kelayos yo'atzos*, the kidneys that give advice, that say yes and no. Every organ the Torah talks about has three parts, corresponding to *Chabad*, *chagas* and *nehi* (the three triads of *sefiros*), and so too the kidney.

blocks.title: Adrenaline and testosterone
blocks.text:
The middle gland is connected not to the brain but to the emotional response. It gives off adrenaline, a *hod* response: when a person is scared and thinks something is bigger than him, he gets fight or flight. He gives up hope, so he is willing to give all his *koach* away; *hod* is like *mesirus nefesh* (self-sacrifice).

It also secretes testosterone, a thing of *netzach*: confidence. That's why teenage boys, with their high testosterone, are cocky, not scared of danger, always doing crazy stuff: it makes a person feel pumped up, that he can take on anything.

sensitivity.reason: Assigns adrenaline and testosterone to two stacked adrenal glands and ties them to hod and netzach as physiology; loose as medicine, and a reader may take it as fact.
sensitivity.publishable: When a person is scared and thinks something is bigger than him, that is *hod*: he gives up hope, so he is willing to give all his *koach* away; *hod* is like *mesirus nefesh* (self-sacrifice). When a person feels confident and pumped up, that he can take on anything, like a teenager who is not scared of danger and always doing crazy stuff, that is *netzach*.

blocks.text: The kidney itself strains the blood, saying what is good and what is bad, on the level of *nehi*, just as the digestive system is like *netzach* and *hod*: yes and no. *Netzach* says yes, to give; *hod* says no, to hold back.

Before the giver gives, **when you want to bring across chesed and gevura**: say you decided someone is guilty. You have a verdict, but not yet a sentence: what are we going to do with him? Or there is a problem, and you decided it is bad: how do we get rid of it? *Netzach* and *hod* figure out an *eitza* (counsel).

One counsels being very proactive: that is *netzach*. *Hod* is being reserved, nervous and cautious; sometimes a healthy respect, depending how strong it is. Someone cautious with a gun has a *hod*, a *hoda'a* (acknowledgement) that it is dangerous. But a person with anxiety has too much *hod*, and that is not good.

blocks.title: The zealots in the time of the Beis HaMikdash
blocks.text: And sometimes there is too much *netzach*. The *Biryonim* (the zealots) in the time of the *Beis HaMikdash* wanted to go fight, though the correct thing would have been to wait it out. So there are two sides: be proactive or be more passive; go fight or run away.

phrases.he: וכמו כל שיקול הדעת
phrases.en: and like every *shikul hadaas*

phrases.he: בא בהכרעה
ואחר הכרעה ישקול במאזני צדק שהן נצח והוד, איך להביא השפע למקבל כו'

blocks.text: Every *shikul hadaas* (weighing of the mind) comes to a decision; the whole middle line is weighing and making a judgment call. First you decide the *etzem* thing, whether it is good or bad. Then you decide again how to bring it out: the scales of justice, *netzach* and *hod*, how to bring the flow to the receiver.

sections.title: The middle line is one: it reaches the inner Keser, so it can join the two
sections.summary: *Daas*, *tiferes* and *yesod* are one middle line, like the long bar through the boards of the *Mishkan*: on each level a personal decision between two poles. It can join the lines because it goes up to the inner *Keser*, the goal for which both sides are only tools.

phrases.he: והיינו כללות ענין קו האמצעי דת''י, שמחבר לב' קוין דימין ושמאל

blocks.text: This is the middle line of *daas*, *tiferes* and *yesod*. *Yesod* connects *netzach* and *hod*: you decide what to do from a personal interest and connection. The real teacher is sensitive to the student, relates to him, and tailor-makes the thing for him, like *hashgacha pratis* (individual Divine providence), a personalized connection. *Yesod* decides what is best between the two in this situation.

So a *bar daas* (a person of understanding) appreciates both sides and can still make a human, wise choice. People who give good advice see both sides; they understand where this person is holding, how each method affects different situations, and what is best here. That is the middle line, which connects the two lines of right and left.

phrases.he: ופרטי התכללותן נקרא י''ב גבולי אלכסון כידוע,
phrases.en: And the particular ways that they connect are called the twelve diagonal lines.

phrases.he: וקו האמצעי נקרא בריח התיכון
phrases.en: The middle line is called the support beam,

phrases.he: שמבריח מן הקצה כו'

blocks.title: The twelve edges of a cube
blocks.text: **The particular ways that they connect are called the twelve diagonal lines.** There are two ways to count the twelve. One is a cube's twelve edges. Standing in the middle of the cube you can go north, south, east and west, and up and down: six, like the six *middos*. But you can also go diagonally, northeast or northwest: four on the compass, four up and four down, twelve, like the edges of a cube.

The other way, closer to what he says here: draw the *sefiros* as a *partzuf* in three lines. Seven lines connect them up and down, three across, and twelve diagonally; those twelve are how they are included in each other. The last two run from *bina* to *netzach* and from *chachma* to *hod*.

blocks.title: The middle bar of the Mishkan
blocks.text:
**The middle line is called the support beam**, the *bariach hatichon* (the middle bar), which bolts from end to end. In a house the support beam goes all the way through; you arrange the walls so that it can. In the *Mishkan* each wall had two bars through rings on the outside, top and bottom, and a hole drilled through the center of all the boards, with one long pole through all three walls: the *bariach hatichon*, from end to end.

Look at the *Mishkan* sideways: the right and left lines are separate for each wall, but the middle line goes through everything and stays the same. The middle line is really one *inyan*.

*Daas*, *tiferes* and *yesod*, and also *Keser* and *Malchus*, are really one *sefira*, the middle line: "It's all your personal decision." In *daas* you decide in the intellect, in *tiferes* in the *middos*, in *yesod* for *netzach* and *hod*. On each level there are two poles, and your personal decision is the middle line between them.

blocks.title: The dimmer switch
blocks.text: It is like a light switch that you can turn up and down. Essentially there is all the way off and all the way on, and where you decide to turn it is the middle line.

phrases.he: דהיינו שעולה עד בחינת פנימית הכתר,
phrases.en: and that's the *inyan* that it goes all the way to *pnimiyus haKeser*,

phrases.he: שלמעלה מהתחלקות הקוין
על כן יש בכחו לחבר ולכלול ב' הקוין כו'.
phrases.en: therefore it's able to connect.

blocks.text: That is, it goes all the way up to the *pnimiyus* of the *Keser*. That is why *davka* it can decide: the middle line looks deeper, at what you really want to accomplish, and because you know where you are trying to go, you can find the best way in this situation and go straight to it.

And that is higher than the division into lines. From there *chesed* and *gevura* don't matter: they are *keilim* (vessels), "just a means to an end." Connected to the end, you can find whatever compromise reaches the goal. So *Tikun* comes from higher than *Tohu*, from the *nekuda*, the *pnimiyus*.

So it has the power to join and include the two lines: coming from *b'etzem* (in essence), higher than this *hischalkus* (division), **therefore it's able to connect**.

sections.title: The inner Keser: the revealed will and delight, with a hidden reason
sections.summary: *Keser sheb'Keser* is the will and delight that come out revealed, with ten *sefiros* of their own. Its *chachma* is the *ta'am kamus*, the hidden reason for the will, really a taste of delight; its *middos* are unlimited, an impossible dream, and are called the days of old next to the *middos* of *chachma* and *bina*.

phrases.he: וביאור ענין פנימית הכתר דנאצלים שנקרא כתר שבכתר (והוא בחינת כתר דעתיק יומין ואריך אנפין כו')
היינו בחינת הרצון והתענוג הבא בגלוי,
phrases.en: It's like when you have a revealed desire and a revealed pleasure.

phrases.he: שנקרא אור הכתר,
שגם הוא כלול מעשר ספירות
phrases.en: that this is also has ten *sefiros*.

blocks.text: The *pnimiyus* of the *Keser* of *Atzilus*, called *Keser sheb'Keser*, is like the *Akudim* (the bound lights), the single *nekuda* from before, which includes everything: the will and the delight that come out revealed, a revealed desire and a revealed pleasure. This too has ten *sefiros*.

phrases.he: ובחינת חכמה שבכתר זהו הטעם לרצון
phrases.en: the *chachma* of the *Keser* is the reason for the *ratzon*.

phrases.he: ונקרא טעם כמוס לרצון

blocks.text: The *chachma* of the *Keser* is the reason for the will, called a *ta'am kamus* (a hidden reason) for the will. Here he means the reason that comes after the will. Rabbi Walters thinks it is called hidden because the will usually covers over the reason: even the reason you give for it is not the real reason.

The other reason it is called hidden: the *pnimiyus* of *ta'am* is *ta'am* as delight, a taste, the *geshmak* (relish) that you get. You want this *davka* because it gives you a certain *geshmak*, a special *taanug* (delight), and that is what you are looking for.

blocks.title: Why that flavor ice cream?
blocks.text: So the form you find for your will is your reason. Ask a person, "Why did you pick that flavor ice cream?" "'Cause it's more chocolatey." So what? "That's just telling me what it is." You are looking for a certain *geshmak*, and the reason only pinpoints which aspect is the thing you want.

phrases.he: וכן יש בו חסד ונצח
phrases.en: and it also has *chesed* and *netzach*,

phrases.he: והכל בבחינת הרצון שהוא בלתי מוגבל,
phrases.en: and the *ratzon*, it's not limited.

phrases.he: גם שבא בגלוי מעצם העלם הרצון כנזכר לעיל

blocks.text: It also has *chesed* and *netzach*: everything is in the will, and all of it unlimited, even though it came out revealed from the essential concealment of the will. It already went through *Adam Kadmon* and became a will for a particular thing: instead of a will for a home, now a will for a house. But it is still unlimited, still unreasonable.

blocks.title: The impossible mansion
blocks.text: A house is realistic, tangible, in theory desirable in the physical world. But in the *Keser* he wants a mansion that is totally impossible to get, a palace infinitely big and infinitely rich. So with everything: from the essential will, a person's *chesed*, say his love for his kid, is infinite; he wants to be a *mashpia* (giver) infinitely good.

phrases.he: ועל כן המדות שברצון ותענוג נקרא ימי קדם
phrases.en: that's why they're called the olden days.

phrases.he: לגבי מדות שבחכמה ובינה
phrases.en: compared to the *middos* that come in *chachma* and *bina*

phrases.he: שבאים בהגבלה כפי הגבלת השכל הגלוי בלבד
כמו שיתבאר,
phrases.en: like we'll explain,

phrases.he: עד בחינת מלכות שבכתר
phrases.en: until *Malchus sheb'Keser*.

blocks.text: So the *middos* in the will and delight are called *yemei kedem*, the olden days. Like everything was bigger in the olden days: you went ten miles to school, and both ways were uphill. "I don't know, maybe it's connected; it's interesting that they call them old."

Compared to the *middos* in *chachma* and *bina*, which think what is practical, these are *kedem*, primal: your essential desire before you get practical. As the *ratzon kadum* (the primordial will) is the days of old relative to *Adam Kadmon*, this is the days of old relative to *chachma* and *bina*: "your original dream." *Chachma* and *bina* bring it down to scale, to what is possible, within the limits of the revealed intellect alone, down to *Malchus sheb'Keser*.

sections.title: Above the division: the will with no reason, and the curtain before it
sections.summary: The outer *Keser* divides into lines because a reason gives the will a form, with better and worse. The *Keser sheb'Keser* is a simple will with no reason, all or nothing, like G-d's "Be silent, so it arose in thought". The *paroches* between it and *chachma* is where the will takes a form, so prayer goes before it to change judgement to kindness.

phrases.he: ומבחינת חיצוניות דכתר נחלק לג' קוין
phrases.en: and from the *chitzoniyus* of the *Keser* though it already divides into three *kavin*.

phrases.he: מפני שבטעם הכמוס לרצון נקרא התחלקות הרצון לחסד וגבורה וממוצע כו'

blocks.text: But from the *chitzoniyus* of the *Keser* it already divides into three lines, because in the hidden reason for the will the division of the will into *chesed*, *gevura* and an intermediary is recognizable. (He reads the text's *nikra*, "is called", as *nikar*, "is recognizable".)

Once you make a *tzura* (form) of what you want, the reason, there is already something you like and something you don't, better or worse, closer or farther. *Chachma* and *bina* figure out what you can practically get that is the closest match to your will. So from the *chitzoniyus* it already has a form. Even an unpractical one lets you say, "Okay, I want a huge mansion, so we'll get you the biggest thing we can find." From there you can have a *Tikun* thing, a decision on the three lines.

phrases.he: אבל בכתר שבכתר שלמעלה מטעם כמוס לרצון עדיין,
phrases.en: but the *Keser* *Keser* is higher than any particular *ratzon*,

phrases.he: רק רצון פשוט ועצמי בלא טעם כלל
כי אין טעם לרצון כלל, גם לא טעם כמוס

blocks.text: But the *Keser sheb'Keser* is higher than any particular will: only a simple, essential will, with no reason at all. From the essential will there is no compromise; it is all or nothing: as for your inner goal, either you got it or you didn't.

For there is no reason for the will at all. Why do you want it? The real inner thing, you just want because you want it. Once you start figuring out that you want it like this, you attach your essential will to a particular form.

blocks.title: The will for money and the get-rich-quick tapes
blocks.text: Not really an essential will, but relatively: say the will for money. That is the essential will, in a *nekuda*, higher than every reason: you want it because you want it. Then in the *chitzoniyus*, *chachma* and *bina* start to picture how you will get it, say a business deal; you go to one of these get-rich-quick tapes and they get you all psyched up on how much money you'll make. Even a totally impractical dream is already a particular way to get it: it is already coming into a line.

He already sees that some things are closer to what he wants and some farther, so he has to make it *davka* in a form that fits the will. From the side of the essential will it is not like that: only a simple, essential will, with no reason at all, for there is no reason in the will at all, not even a hidden reason.

phrases.he: כענין שתוק כך עלה במחשבה כו', וכמו שכתוב במקום אחר

blocks.text: Like "Be silent, so it arose in thought", said of the ten martyrs of the kingdom: that is not a thing to compromise on; that is what He wanted. Were it a means to an end, you could say, "Well, I have a better way for you to do it." Since it was the thing itself He wanted, there is no compromise.

Like "This is the statute of the Torah" of the *para aduma* (the red heifer). One explanation the Rebbe gives: why you need a *yerida* (a descent) for an *aliya* (an ascent) is the *chok* (a commandment done just because G-d said so), why one person becomes *tamei* (impure) to make the other *tahor* (pure). We understand that is how the world works: to have an ascent you need a descent.

blocks.title: Profit and the sink
blocks.text: If you want to make a profit, you have to invest money. If you are going to fix your sink, you are going to get your hands dirty. Fine, that's the way it works.

blocks.question: Why did G-d have to make it that way?
blocks.text: G-d didn't have to make it "no pain, no gain"; He could have given us all the virtues. All these explanations say *nahama d'kisufa* (the bread of shame), but He could have given us the virtue without it. That is the *chok*: G-d chose to do it like this. That is the real essential will, the essential delight; here, the fiftieth gate, the essential thing you cannot describe, as explained elsewhere.

phrases.he: על כן הוא למעלה מהתחלקות ימין ושמאל כו', הגם שבא בגלוי מבחינת האחרונה שבהעלם הרצון דבחינת אדם קדמון (כנזכר לעיל בסוף אות י''ט)

blocks.question: "Wait a minute, but it already has an order from *Adam Kadmon*. *Adam Kadmon* already makes three lines."
blocks.text: So it is above the division into right and left, even though it comes out revealed from the last level of the concealed will of *Adam Kadmon*. Take the will for money: to get there you already made three lines in *Adam Kadmon*, working out your self-image; from your essential desire to be happy came an image of prosperity, of which being rich is a part. So it is already divided into lines.

True, relative to the essential will before *Adam Kadmon* it became lines. But once it comes out, relative to what follows it is an essential will again: that is *gilui ha'helem* (revelation of what is hidden), the essence connected with this thing. As long as that doesn't change, it has the full force of an essential will. You want happiness; if your *Adam Kadmon* tells you happiness means money, you want money, *nekuda*, as they say in Hebrew. And that is not negotiable.

The same is how a Jew can have *mesirus nefesh* for a *mitzva* (a commandment). What a Jew really wants is to be connected to G-d. If a prophet told you to transgress any *mitzva* in the Torah, it would be a *mitzva* to do it. So you don't essentially want to keep Shabbos: if a prophet said to desecrate it, or in *pikuach nefesh* (danger to life), it is a *mitzva* to desecrate Shabbos.

How can a Jew, when a *goy* says, "I'm gonna shoot you if you're not *mechalel Shabbos*," have *mesirus nefesh* for it? While the Torah says that here this connects to G-d, it carries the full force of his will to be connected to G-d; where the Torah says it doesn't, he can do it and stay connected. Once he associates the two, the full force of his *yechida* (the essence of the soul) is in every deed: totally non-negotiable, only the essential will, not the three *mochin*.

sensitivity.reason: Uses the word goy for the non-Jew who threatens a Jew, a word many readers take as dismissive; the series flags the word wherever it occurs.
sensitivity.publishable: How can a Jew, when a non-Jew says, "I'm gonna shoot you if you're not *mechalel Shabbos*," have *mesirus nefesh* for it? While the Torah says that here this connects to G-d, it carries the full force of his will to be connected to G-d; where the Torah says it doesn't, he can do it and stay connected. Once he associates the two, the full force of his *yechida* (the essence of the soul) is in every deed: totally non-negotiable, only the essential will, not the three *mochin*.

phrases.he: ועל זה אמר והבדילה הפרוכת בין הקדש כו'
phrases.en: the *paroches* separates between the *Kodesh* and the *Kodesh Kodashim*,

phrases.he: בחינת פרסא שבין כתר דכתר לחכמה כו'
והוא בחינת קרומא דאוירא
phrases.en: This is the membrane of air, the arachnoid membrane in the brain, it's called,

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב במקום אחר באריכות

blocks.text: About this it says, "The *paroches* (the curtain) shall separate between the Holy" and the Holy of Holies: between the *Keser* of *Keser*, the essential will, and the *chachma* of the will, where it already has a form. There is a *masach* (a screen): the *parsa* (the partition) between *Keser* of *Keser* and *chachma*.

It is the *kruma d'avira*, the membrane of air, called the arachnoid membrane in the brain, as is written elsewhere at length. We will talk about it in chapter 25, where you can talk about the hairs, *Atik*, and the thirteen tikkunim of the beard of *Arich*.

blocks.title: The fluid of delight under the skull
blocks.text: Physically, a liquid under the skull, in medicine, he thinks, the subdural fluid, is the essential delight: it gives a person the essential feeling of delight and will. It doesn't come down pure: a spongy membrane holds it, and little hair-like tubes inject it into the brain. An active part of the brain draws more of it and is stimulated; dripping on the back of the spine, it gives the person delight.

sensitivity.reason: Says a fluid under the skull is the source of delight, injected into the brain and dripping on the spine, as medical fact; not what medicine says, and a reader may take it as fact.
sensitivity.publishable: The point is that the essential delight does not come down to the faculties in its pure form. A membrane holds it and lets it through, and wherever a faculty is active, more of the delight is drawn into it and stimulates it.

blocks.title: Each person's membrane, each person's nature
blocks.text: It drips according to the shape of this membrane, and each person's is shaped a little differently. That gives a person his nature: he enjoys certain things more and is better at certain things, because he gets delight more easily from certain parts of his brain, from certain forms. That is the *inyan* of the *mazal* (lit. a flow), the *mazalos*: *mazal* comes from *nozel*, flowing, which we can talk about in chapter 25.

sensitivity.reason: Continues the physiology of the brain fluid, making the shape of the membrane the cause of a person's nature, as medical fact.
sensitivity.publishable: The delight comes through according to the shape of this membrane, and each person's is a little different. That gives a person his nature: he enjoys certain things more and is better at certain things, because he gets delight more easily from certain forms. That is the *inyan* of the *mazal* (lit. a flow), the *mazalos*: *mazal* comes from *nozel*, flowing, which we can talk about in chapter 25.

blocks.text: So the point is that this *masach* is what connects: to go from the essential will to the means to the end, you have to create a thing that connects your essential will to a form, as is written elsewhere at length.

phrases.he: ועל כן אומר יהי רצון מלפניך, מלפני הפרסא כו'
לשנות מרצון של דין לרצון של חסד וכהאי גוונא כו' ודי למבין:

blocks.text: So one says, "May it be the will before You", before the *parsa*. When we want something changed we *davka* connect to the essential will, higher than any form; there it can come out in any form, and G-d can accomplish the same thing in a totally different way. But once it comes through the *paroches* it gets set in a certain form, because that is already a reason for the will.

To change from a will of *din* to a will of *chesed*, and the like, and this is enough for one who understands. That is why *davka* the essential will, the essence of the *Keser*, can change from *din* to *chesed*: it can go either way. That is the *inyan* of the three *mochin*.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does *chachma* lean towards *chesed* and *bina* towards *gevura*? Use the gift and the person who is "just misguided".
Why is *netzach* "separate" from *chesed*, and what does *mivtzaim* in the cold show about it?
What does *daas* do with the two ways of looking at a person, and why can a computer not do it?
How is *tiferes* like mercy after the verdict, and what is the attribute of Yaakov?
Why can the middle line join the two lines, and what does the middle bar of the *Mishkan* show about it?
Why is there no compromise in the *Keser sheb'Keser*, and why does prayer go "before the *parsa*"?

notes.text: Line 27: he reads "it is Keser of Adam Kadmon" (79 w1465-1477) where the text has "Keser of Atik Yomin and Arich Anpin"; and in line 28 he reads "which is called Arich Anpin" (79 w1494-1502) where the text has "called the light of the Keser". The block follows the chapter's text and his explanation (the Akudim, the single nekuda) without naming either reading.
Line 34: he reads the text's nikra as nikar ("recognizable") and says it is "supposed to be" so (79 w2223-2241); the block says so. The transcript hears the two words the same and is garbled here.

The physiology in classes 78 (the kidney and adrenal glands, adrenaline and testosterone, 78 w2122-2423) and 80 (a fluid under the skull, which he calls subdural, as the essential delight dripping on the spine, 80 w1368-1606) is kept as he gave it, with his own hedges ("from what I researched", "I think"). It is loose as anatomy (the adrenal glands are not two glands stacked on the kidney; the subdural space normally holds no fluid; the fluid around the brain is cerebrospinal fluid, under the arachnoid). Those blocks are flagged health-or-legal, as chapter 15 flags his medical claims, with publishable texts that keep the hod/netzach and the membrane points.

Phrases he reads without translating keep their Hebrew alone: the start of line 1, line 2 up to Keser sheb'Keser (he explains it instead), the end of line 3 and all of line 4, the end of line 7 (b'davar murkav, which he glosses as "not an etzem chesed"), the end of line 8, the end of line 9, the start of lines 11 and 13, lines 14, 16 and 23 (read whole, then explained), most of line 15 and line 19, the middle of line 20, the end of line 21, line 22, the end of line 24, the end of line 25, line 27 and the middle of line 28, the end of line 29 and of line 31, the middle of line 32, line 34, the end of line 35, all of line 36 (his "why do you want it? You want it because you want it" explains it rather than translating it), lines 37 and 38, line 40, the end of line 41, and lines 42-43. The English of line 13 ("it's davka the middle thing, which is daas", 78 w366-373) is from his summary after the opening question; the end of line 12 (78 w6-14) is from class 78's opening, and the English of the end of line 20 is from class 79's opening (79 w11-20). The English of line 26 is the end of the sentence right after his reading of it (79 w1460-1464); the first half of that sentence ("since it's coming from b'etzem, it's higher than this hischalkus") gives the reason and belongs to line 25, so it is in the block, not the phrase.

In the mesirus nefesh block (80 w1142-1176) the transcript has "the whole inyan of shin-samech-heh kedushos", which is garbled (perhaps the 365 prohibitions); the block keeps only his point that the Torah tells a Jew where a deed is not connected to his connection to G-d.
